title: The beginnings of modern cognition

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists excavating a cave in South Africa some years ago unearthed an unusual shell inside was a rusty red substance. After analysing the mixture and nearby stone tools, they realised they had found the world's earliest known paint, made 100,000 years ago from charcoal, animal bones, and iron-rich rock. The shell was a storage container – a prehistoric paint can. The find revealed more than just the act that people used paints so long ago – it provided a glimpse into the minds of early humans. Combining materials to create a product that doesn't resemble the original ingredients and saving it for later suggests its creators were capable of abstract thinking and preparing for the future.

These are among the mental abilities that many anthropologists say distinguished humans, Homo sapiens, from earlier species. Yet they have no agreed-upon definition of exactly what makes human cognition our mental processes-so special, ‘it's hard enough to tell what the cognitive abilities are of somebody who's standing in front of you,’ says Alison Brooks, of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D. C. ‘So it's really hard to tell for someone who's been dead half a million years.’ What anthropologists can do, however, is examine the artefacts such people left behind. When new technologies or behaviours appear in the archaeological record, anthropologists try to determine what sort of novel thinking was required to fashion a spear, say, or mix paint. The past few decades have been particularly fruitful for finding such evidence and archaeologists are now piecing together these patterns of behavior to try to find out how and when humans started to think and act like modem people.

In the 1970s, it looked like there was a simple answer: modern cognition evolved in Europe 40,000 years ago. That's when cave art, jewellery and sculpted figurines all seemed to appear for the first time. The art was a sign that humans could use symbols to represent their world and themselves, archaeologists reasoned, and therefore probably had language, too. One problem with this analysis was that the earliest fossils of modern humans dated from as many as 200,000 years ago. Richard Klein, a palaeoanthropologist at Stanford University, suggested that a genetic mutation occurred about 40,000 years ago, and caused an abrupt revolution in people's cognition and behaviour.

In the decades following, however, archaeologists working in Africa overturned the notion that there was a gap between when the human body evolved and when modern thinking emerged. ‘As researchers began to more intensely investigate regions outside of Europe, indications of symbolic behaviour got older and older,’ says archaeologist April Nowell of the University of Victoria in Canada. Now many anthropologists agree that modem cognition was probably in place when Homo sapiens emerged.

Curtis Marean, a paleoanthropologist at Arizona State University, thinks symbolic thinking was a crucial change in the evolution of the human mind. ‘When you have that, you have the ability to develop language,’ he says. He also believes symbolic thinking aided the formation of the extended social and trading networks which enabled humans to spread into new, more complex environments, such as coastal locales, and eventually across the entire planet. ‘But symbolic thinking may not account for all of the changes in the human mind,’ says Thomas Wynn of the University of Colorado. He suggests that advanced ‘working memory’ was the final critical step toward modern cognition. Working memory allows the brain to retrieve, process and retain several chunks of information all at one time to complete a task.

Finding evidence of this kind of cognition is challenging, yet their artefacts that seem to relate to it, such as tools – like a bow and arrow that are composed of separate pieces. But the most convincing example, according to Wynn, may be animal traps. With a trap, the hunter has to think up a device that can catch and hold an animal, and then remember to return later to see whether it worked. Archaeologists in South Africa have recently found clues that humans were using traps to hunt large numbers of small, and sometimes dangerous, forest animals more than 70,000 years ago.

Another area that needs more investigation is what happened after modern cognition evolved. Some archaeologists see a slow progression in the accumulation of knowledge, while others see modern behavior evolving in a fragmented way – stopping and starting over time. Archaeologist Francesco d'Errico of the University of Bordeaux suggests certain advances appear early in the archaeological record only to vanish for tens of thousands of years, before these behaviours get permanently incorporated into the human repertoire about 40,000 years ago. ‘It's probably due to climatic changes, environmental variability and population size,’ d'Errico says. He also notes that several tool technologies and aspects of symbolic expression, such as engraved artefacts, seem to drop out of sight around 70,000 years ago. The timing coincides with a global cold spell, when populations probably dwindled and fragmented in response to the change in climate. Perhaps the best way to settle whether the build-up of modern behaviour was steady or punctuated is to find more archaeological sites to fill in the gaps. There are only a handful of sites, for example, that cover the beginning of human history, between 125,000 and 250,000 years ago. If more of these were found many more questions could be answered.
